items.abstract:
<jats:p><div>
 Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) treats memory as a retrieval problem: store content, embed it, fetch what is relevant. This suffices for static knowledge bases but breaks down for agents that learn over time, where stored information contradicts itself, beliefs evolve, and corrections must propagate through dependent reasoning. Current architectures commit a category error, applying uniform persistence semantics to information with fundamentally different epistemic status.
</div>
<div>
 <br>
</div>
<div>
 We introduce Layered Epistemic Agent Protocol (LeAP), a framework that treats agent memory as an epistemology problem. LeAP formalizes stratified epistemic types with distinct evidence requirements: observations require no justification, claims require single sources, facts require corroboration, and beliefs require derivation chains. The framework defines warrant functions, coherence invariants, and a revision protocol satisfying AGM belief revision postulates. Coherence is decidable for finite stores.
</div>
<div>
 <br>
</div>
<div>
 We present CITE (Context In Tiered Epistemology), a four-layer architecture implementing LeAP. Its layers (Memory, Knowledge, Wisdom, and Intelligence) enforce distinct persistence semantics: decay-based, supersession-based, evidence-gated, and session-scoped respectively. Write-time validations gate every entry by epistemic layer, preventing contradiction accumulation at the source rather than detecting it after retrieval.
</div>
<div>
 <br>
</div>
<div>
 In a design validation on 500 annotated coding-agent sessions, CITE achieves 95% contradiction detection compared to 66% for an embedding-only baseline, and 87% revision propagation compared to 12%.
</div></jats:p>
title: Beyond Retrieval: Layered Epistemic Agent Protocol for Memory Coherence

items.abstract: <jats:p>Enterprise deployments of Retrieval-Augmented Generation and multi-agent LLM systems routinely handle data subject to role-based access control, yet the semantic retrieval step in these pipelines bypasses conventional authorization enforcement. We formalize this gap as a pipeline ordering problem: once unauthorized content enters any model context, no downstream filter can provably undo its influence on generation. We introduce Authorization-First Retrieval (AFR), an architectural invariant requiring that authorization constrain the retrieval candidate set before any learned component consumes retrieved content. We prove AFR is a necessary condition for authorization correctness under the contextexposure model used by all major deployed RAG systems. We construct a controlled evaluation corpus of 43 chunks across 28 documents with role-scoped access rules spanning five enterprise roles, three sensitivity levels, and four domains. Against 93 structured queries covering six attack categories, retrieve-then-filter pipelines expose unauthorized context in 96.8% of queries and violate authorization correctness on 100% of queries that should be denied. AFR eliminates all structural leaks (0/93) and all answer leaks (0/93). A chunk-size sweep across five granularities confirms AFR holds invariant to chunking strategy, while retrieve-then-filter leakage increases monotonically with chunk size. Stress testing at retrieval depth exceeding corpus size shows AFR holds under worstcase saturation. We identify parametric knowledge leakage as a fundamental boundary on what retrieval architecture can guarantee.</jats:p>
title: Authorization-First Retrieval: Enforcing Least Privilege in Multi-Agent RAG Systems

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large Language Models (LLMs) face fundamental challenges in long-context reasoning: many documents exceed their finite context windows, while performance on texts that do fit degrades with sequence length, necessitating their augmentation with external memory frameworks. Current solutions, which have evolved from retrieval using semantic embeddings to more sophisticated structured knowledge graphs representations for improved sense-making and associativity, are tailored for fact-based retrieval and fail to build the space-time-anchored narrative representations required for tracking entities through episodic events. To bridge this gap, we propose the Generative Semantic Workspace (GSW), a neuro-inspired generative memory framework that builds structured, interpretable representations of evolving situations, enabling LLMs to reason over evolving roles, actions, and spatiotemporal contexts. Our framework comprises an Operator, which maps incoming observations to intermediate semantic structures, and a Reconciler, which integrates these into a persistent workspace that enforces temporal, spatial, and logical coherence. On the Episodic Memory Benchmark (EpBench) comprising corpora ranging from 100k to 1M tokens in length, GSW outperforms existing RAG based baselines by up to 20%. Furthermore, GSW is highly efficient, reducing query-time context tokens by 51% compared to the next most token-efficient baseline, reducing inference time costs considerably. More broadly, GSW offers a concrete blueprint for endowing LLMs with human-like episodic memory, paving the way for more capable agents that can reason over long horizons.</jats:p>
title: Beyond Fact Retrieval: Episodic Memory for RAG with Generative Semantic Workspaces
